title: The wheeze has gone quiet
objective: Manage pediatric status asthmaticus with frequent or continuous bronchodilator, early systemic corticosteroid and IV magnesium, and recognize fatigue and rising PaCO2 as signs of impending failure
secondaryObjectives: Recognize and manage acute respiratory failure, acute respiratory infection and ARDS

brief.situation: 02:00 in the PICU. You are the nurse for Leo, 7 years old, admitted at midnight with status asthmaticus. He is on continuous nebulized albuterol through a mask; the ordered IV corticosteroid was given at 00:30 and IV magnesium at 01:00.
handover: At midnight he was wheezing loudly, sitting forward and talking in short phrases.
His mother says he 'finally calmed down and is resting' and asks for the lights off.

Unit policy: the nurse checks a venous or capillary blood gas on the standing order for worsening distress, keeps the continuous nebulizer running, and calls the intensivist at once for decreased air movement, a falling level of consciousness or a rising CO2; sedatives are not given to an asthmatic who is not intubated.
howItWorks: The clock runs in simulated time; study pace runs three simulated minutes per real minute. Pause any time.
Each check takes the time on its button. Decide what the findings mean, what to stop or start, and who must know.
Partway through you are asked to write your reasoning. A debrief scores what you did.

why.question: Why is Leo quieter, and what do you do?

parts.label: What and why
parts.criteria: In status asthmaticus a quiet chest with poor air entry, drowsiness, a smaller pulsus without improvement and a rising PCO2 mean fatigue and impending respiratory failure, not recovery.
parts.modelAnswer: He's not better, he's tiring. The chest is quiet because almost no air is moving, he's drowsy, the pulsus is shrinking without him improving, and his CO2 is 62 and rising.

parts.label: What I do
parts.criteria: Keeps him upright on the continuous nebulizer, checks consciousness and a gas, prepares airway equipment, calls the intensivist at once; no sedation.
parts.modelAnswer: Sit him up, keep the albuterol going, check the gas, get the airway cart in, and call the intensivist now. No sedative.

arrest.headline: Respiratory arrest
arrest.body: A quiet chest with drowsiness in status asthmaticus is impending failure, not improvement. Check the gas, keep the bronchodilator going, never sedate, and call.

safe.headline: Failure caught early
safe.body: You read the quiet chest and drowsiness as tiring, confirmed a rising CO2, kept the nebulizer going, avoided sedation, prepared the airway and called within minutes. That is the expert path.

scoring.modelReasoning: In pediatric status asthmaticus, the danger signs are a quiet chest from airway obstruction so severe that little air moves, drowsiness (altered mental status in young children), a falling pulsus paradoxus without clinical improvement (fatigue) and a rising CO2. Leo has all of them despite continuous albuterol, an early IV corticosteroid and IV magnesium. Keep him upright on the bronchodilator, check a gas, prepare airway equipment and call the intensivist at once for escalation; never sedate a tiring asthmatic who is not intubated, and remember intubation itself carries a high arrest risk.

co2Q.ask: While support is set up: what predicts impending failure?

choices.label: A rising CO2, drowsiness and fatigue

co2Q.explain: Monitoring CO2 is a useful indicator of impending failure; drowsiness and a resolving pulsus without improvement suggest fatigue.
